flows.name: Old Assyrian donkey caravans, Assur to Kanesh
flows.note: Family firms in Assur sent black donkeys loaded with about 65 kg of tin and textiles each across the Jazira and the Taurus; agents in the karum at Kanesh sold the cargo, the donkeys too, and sent silver home; winter snows closed the passes.

sources.cite: Klaas R. Veenhof, Aspects of Old Assyrian Trade and its Terminology (1972)
Mogens Trolle Larsen, Ancient Kanesh: A Merchant Colony in Bronze Age Anatolia (2015)
Gojko Barjamovic, A Historical Geography of Anatolia in the Old Assyrian Colony Period (2011)
Wikipedia: Kültepe

flows.estimate_note: Trip of about six weeks from the letters; caravans per year and party size estimated from the 23,000 tablets (Larsen).

flows.name: Gulf ships from Ur to Dilmun, Magan and Meluhha
flows.note: Alik-Dilmun merchants of Ur, like Ea-nasir, shipped textiles and silver down the Gulf and brought back copper bought at Dilmun; ships from Meluhha (the Indus) are said in Sargon's inscription to moor at Akkad. Counts are estimates.

sources.cite: A. Leo Oppenheim, 'The Seafaring Merchants of Ur', Journal of the American Oriental Society 74 (1954)
Wikipedia: Dilmun
Wikipedia: Meluhha

flows.name: Egyptian royal expeditions to Punt
flows.note: Ships were built on the Nile, carried in pieces across the desert from Coptos to the Red Sea shore and reassembled; Hatshepsut's fleet of five ships (c. 1470 BCE) is shown at Deir el-Bahari. Expeditions came years or decades apart, so per_year is an average.

sources.cite: Kathryn A. Bard and Rodolfo Fattovich, Seafaring Expeditions to Punt in the Middle Kingdom (2018)
Wikipedia: Land of Punt

flows.name: Late Bronze Age copper ships, Ugarit to Cyprus, Crete and the Aegean
flows.note: Coasting ships like the Uluburun wreck (c. 1320 BCE, ten tons of copper, a ton of tin) worked round the eastern Mediterranean in the sailing season; numbers of ships are estimated.

sources.cite: Cemal Pulak, 'The Uluburun shipwreck: an overview', International Journal of Nautical Archaeology 27 (1998)
Wikipedia: Uluburun shipwreck

flows.name: Phoenician silver and tin voyages to Gadir and Tartessos
flows.note: Tyrian ships coasted west by stages, wintering at colonies if need be, to buy the silver of the Rio Tinto through Gadir; voyage counts and times are estimates (the Old Testament 'ships of Tarshish' made the trip in a three-year cycle).

sources.cite: Maria Eugenia Aubet, The Phoenicians and the West (2nd ed., 2001)
Wikipedia: Tartessos

flows.name: Greek colonising expeditions (apoikiai) to Sicily and Italy
goods_out: sacred fire from the mother city
flows.note: A founder (oikistes) sent with Delphi's sanction led a few hundred young men in penteconters to found a new city, as Archias did from Corinth to Syracuse in 733 BCE; party size and frequency are estimates.

sources.cite: John Boardman, The Greeks Overseas (4th ed., 1999)
Wikipedia: Greek colonisation

flows.name: Black Sea grain ships to Athens
flows.note: Athens lived on imported wheat, much of it from the Bosporan kingdom; Demosthenes says 400,000 medimnoi came from there a year, and Philip II seized 230 grain ships off Hieron in 340 BCE.

sources.cite: Demosthenes, Against Leptines 31-33
Philochorus, FGrHist 328 F 162 (seizure of the grain fleet, 340 BCE)
Peter Garnsey, Famine and Food Supply in the Graeco-Roman World (1988)

flows.name: Achaemenid royal couriers (angareion) on the Royal Road
flows.note: Herodotus counts 111 staging posts over 2,500 km and says a man on foot took 90 days, while relays of mounted couriers 'stayed by neither snow nor rain' passed messages station to station; the courier time and frequency are estimates.

sources.cite: Herodotus, Histories 5.52-54 and 8.98
Pierre Briant, From Cyrus to Alexander (2002), ch. 9
Wikipedia: Royal Road

flows.name: Travellers on foot along the Persian Royal Road
flows.note: Herodotus gives three months at 150 stades a day from Sardis to Susa; the Persepolis Fortification tablets record parties drawing rations on sealed travel documents. Party counts are estimates.

sources.cite: Herodotus, Histories 5.53
Richard T. Hallock, Persepolis Fortification Tablets (1969)

flows.name: Frankincense caravans from South Arabia to Gaza
flows.note: Pliny says frankincense went from Thomna to Gaza in 65 camel stages, 2,437 Roman miles, paying dues all the way; caravan counts and size are estimates.

sources.cite: Pliny the Elder, Natural History 12.32 (63-65)
Wikipedia: Incense Route

flows.name: Roman grain fleet, Alexandria to Puteoli and Ostia (annona)
flows.note: Big freighters carried Egypt's tax wheat (about a third of Rome's grain, says Josephus) against the northwesterlies, slowly round by Lycia and Crete, then ran home to Alexandria in two or three weeks; St Paul's grain ship carried 276 people. Ship-voyages per year are estimated from the grain tonnage.

sources.cite: Lionel Casson, Ships and Seamanship in the Ancient World (1971), pp. 297-299
Josephus, Jewish War 2.386
Acts 27
Wikipedia: Cura Annonae

flows.name: Egyptian grain fleet to Constantinople
flows.note: Justinian's Edict 13 fixed Egypt's grain levy for the capital at 8 million artabas a year; ships waited at Tenedos for a south wind to beat up the Hellespont. Ship counts are estimates; the Persian conquest of Egypt in 618 ended it.

sources.cite: Justinian, Edict 13 (538/9)
A. H. M. Jones, The Later Roman Empire (1964), ch. 18
Wikipedia: Cura Annonae

flows.name: Roman monsoon ships from the Red Sea to Muziris
flows.note: Strabo saw up to 120 ships a year leave Myos Hormos for India; the Periplus says to leave Egypt in July and Pliny gives 30 days to Ocelis and 40 more across the open sea to Muziris on the southwest monsoon, returning in December-January.

sources.cite: Strabo, Geography 2.5.12
Periplus of the Erythraean Sea 39, 49, 56 (Lionel Casson, trans., 1989)
Pliny the Elder, Natural History 6.101-106
Wikipedia: Muziris

flows.crew_note: party includes crew and the archers Pliny says were carried against pirates

flows.name: Roman imperial post (cursus publicus), Rome to the Rhine
flows.note: Officials and couriers with a diploma changed animals at mutationes and slept at mansiones; Ramsay's study puts ordinary official speed at about 50 Roman miles a day, more in emergencies. Per-year counts are estimates.

sources.cite: A. M. Ramsay, 'The Speed of the Roman Imperial Post', Journal of Roman Studies 15 (1925)
Wikipedia: Cursus publicus

flows.name: Han embassies along the Silk Road to the Western Regions
flows.note: After Zhang Qian, Sima Qian says, the court sent embassies of several hundred, or at least a hundred, men; 'in one year as many as ten or more, and as few as five or six'; the far ones took eight or nine years to come back. The one-way time is an estimate.

sources.cite: Sima Qian, Shiji 123 (Burton Watson, trans., Records of the Grand Historian, 1961)
Valerie Hansen, The Silk Road: A New History (2012)

flows.name: Sogdian merchant caravans, Samarkand to Chang'an
flows.note: Sogdian families ran a diaspora of trading posts from Samarkand to Luoyang (the 'Ancient Letters' of c. 313 come from it); Turfan travel passes show caravans of a few merchants with servants and animals. Caravan counts are estimates.

sources.cite: Étienne de la Vaissière, Sogdian Traders: A History (2005)
Valerie Hansen, The Silk Road: A New History (2012), ch. 4
Wikipedia: Sogdia

flows.name: Tang silk convoys paying the northwest garrisons
flows.note: The Tang paid its Anxi garrisons largely in silk cloth; Hansen cites documents showing roughly 900,000 bolts sent a year to the northwest around 730-755, which in turn fed the oasis markets. Convoy counts are estimates.

sources.cite: Valerie Hansen, The Silk Road: A New History (2012), ch. 3 and 7
Eric Trombert, 'Textiles et tissus sur la route de la soie', in La Serinde, terre d'échanges (2000)

flows.name: Chinese Buddhist pilgrim monks to India overland
flows.note: Monks like Faxian (399) and Xuanzang (629) went in small groups to find complete texts, taking a year or more to reach the Ganges; Faxian set out with four companions. Group counts are estimates.

sources.cite: Faxian, A Record of Buddhist Kingdoms (James Legge, trans., 1886)
Xuanzang, Great Tang Records on the Western Regions (646)
Tansen Sen, Buddhism, Diplomacy and Trade (2003)

flows.name: Buddhist monks by sea from Guangzhou via Srivijaya to Tamralipti
flows.note: Yijing sailed from Guangzhou in the eleventh month of 671 on a Persian ship, studied Sanskrit at Srivijaya and reached Tamralipti in 673; his memoir lists 56 monks who made such journeys, so traffic was a few a year. Times include monsoon waits.

sources.cite: Yijing, Chinese Monks in India (Latika Lahiri, trans., 1986)
Wikipedia: Yijing (monk)

flows.name: Japanese embassy ships to Tang China (kentoshi)
flows.note: About fifteen embassies actually sailed, usually four ships with 500-650 people in all (557 in 717, 651 in 838), carrying students and monks such as Kukai and Ennin; many ships were wrecked. per_year is ships per year averaged over the period.

sources.cite: Charlotte von Verschuer, Across the Perilous Sea: Japanese Trade with China and Korea (2006)
Wikipedia: Japanese missions to Tang China

flows.name: Aksumite traders from Adulis to Arabia and India
flows.note: The Periplus calls Adulis the port of the ivory trade, and Cosmas Indicopleustes (c. 550) tells of Aksumite merchants trading at Taprobane; numbers are estimates.

sources.cite: Periplus of the Erythraean Sea 4-5
Cosmas Indicopleustes, Christian Topography 11
Stuart Munro-Hay, Aksum: An African Civilisation of Late Antiquity (1991)

flows.name: Abbasid postal couriers (barid), Baghdad to Khurasan
goods_back: reports of the sahib al-barid on governors, prices and weather
flows.note: Ibn Khurradadhbih, himself a postmaster, lists the barid stations (930 in all) along the empire's roads; relays of mules and riders carried official mail and intelligence. Times and counts are estimates.

sources.cite: Ibn Khurradadhbih, Kitab al-Masalik wa'l-Mamalik (c. 870)
Adam J. Silverstein, Postal Systems in the Pre-Modern Islamic World (2007)
Wikipedia: Barid

flows.name: Radhanite Jewish merchants between Francia and China
flows.note: Ibn Khurradadhbih describes Jewish merchants speaking Arabic, Persian, Greek, Frankish, Spanish and Slavic who sailed from the land of the Franks to Farama, carried goods by camel to the Red Sea and sailed on to India and China. Counts and times are estimates.

sources.cite: Ibn Khurradadhbih, Kitab al-Masalik wa'l-Mamalik (c. 870)
Wikipedia: Radhanite

flows.name: Rus traders down the Volga to Bulghar and the Caspian
flows.note: Ibn Fadlan met Rus merchants at Bulghar in 922 who built wooden houses on the river and sold fur and captives for silver; hundreds of thousands of Islamic dirhams in Baltic hoards date the trade. Boat counts and times are estimates.

sources.cite: Ibn Fadlan, Mission to the Volga (James E. Montgomery, trans., 2017)
Thomas S. Noonan, The Islamic World, Russia and the Vikings, 750-900 (1998)
Wikipedia: Volga trade route

flows.name: Rus monoxyla convoys down the Dnieper to Constantinople
flows.note: Constantine VII describes the dugouts gathering at Kiev in June, portaging the seven rapids under Pecheneg threat and coasting to Constantinople; the treaties of 911 and 944 let at most 50 Rus enter the city at a time. Boat counts are estimates.

sources.cite: Constantine Porphyrogenitus, De Administrando Imperio, ch. 9 (Gy. Moravcsik and R. Jenkins, trans., 1967)
Wikipedia: Trade route from the Varangians to the Greeks

flows.name: Norse ships to Iceland and Greenland
flows.note: Landnámabók records hundreds of settlers sailing to Iceland after 870; later only a few ships a year, and by the 1300s a single royal knarr, sailed to Greenland. Counts are estimates.

sources.cite: Landnámabók
Kirsten A. Seaver, The Frozen Echo: Greenland and the Exploration of North America (1996)
Wikipedia: Norse colonization of North America

flows.name: Trans-Saharan caravans, Sijilmasa to Awdaghust and Ghana
flows.note: Al-Bakri (1068) gives about two months from Sijilmasa to Awdaghust across the desert; Ibn Hawqal saw a cheque of 42,000 dinars drawn there; caravans set out in the cool season. Caravan counts are estimates.

sources.cite: al-Bakri, Kitab al-Masalik wa'l-Mamalik (1068), in N. Levtzion and J. F. P. Hopkins, Corpus of Early Arabic Sources for West African History (1981)
Wikipedia: Trans-Saharan trade

flows.name: Caravans from Sijilmasa via Taghaza to Walata and Mali
flows.note: Ibn Battuta left Sijilmasa in February 1352 with a caravan, reached Taghaza in 25 days and Walata two months after leaving it; salt slabs from Taghaza were cash in Mali. Caravan counts are estimates.

sources.cite: Ibn Battuta, Rihla (H. A. R. Gibb and C. F. Beckingham, trans., vol. 4, 1994)
Nehemia Levtzion, Ancient Ghana and Mali (1973)

flows.name: Azalai salt caravans, Timbuktu to Taoudenni
flows.note: After Moroccan troops destroyed Taghaza (1585) the mines moved to Taoudenni; the great azalai went twice a year, early winter and spring, and the French counted 20,000 camels in 1906 and 8,000 in 1948. party counts people (about one driver for 4 camels, estimated).

sources.cite: E. Ann McDougall, 'The Sahara Reconsidered', African Economic History 12 (1983)
Wikipedia: Azalai

flows.name: Caravans between Tripoli, Fezzan and Bornu
flows.note: The shortest Sahara crossing ran through Fezzan and Kawar to Lake Chad; Barth and Nachtigal travelled it in the 1850s-1860s, and it carried many of the enslaved people taken north across the desert. Caravan counts are estimates.

sources.cite: Heinrich Barth, Travels and Discoveries in North and Central Africa (1857-58)
Ralph A. Austen, Trans-Saharan Africa in World History (2010)

flows.name: Forty Days Road caravans, Darfur to Asyut
flows.note: W. G. Browne crossed with the Darfur caravan in 1793; the yearly caravan could reach several thousand camels and carried thousands of enslaved Sudanese north to Egypt. party counts traders, drivers and captives together (estimated).

sources.cite: W. G. Browne, Travels in Africa, Egypt and Syria (1799)
Terence Walz, Trade between Egypt and Bilad as-Sudan, 1700-1820 (1978)
Wikipedia: Darb al-Arba'in

flows.name: Hausa kola caravans, Kano to Salaga
flows.note: Each dry season caravans of hundreds to over a thousand people, with donkeys and head porters, walked from Hausaland to the Asante kola markets; Lovejoy reconstructs their organisation from traders' accounts. Counts are estimates.

sources.cite: Paul E. Lovejoy, Caravans of Kola: The Hausa Kola Trade, 1700-1900 (1980)

flows.name: Gold caravans from the Zimbabwe plateau to Sofala
flows.note: Gold from the plateau went down to Sofala, where Kilwa's agents shipped it north; the trip was made on foot in the dry season with head porters. Group counts and times are estimates.

sources.cite: Innocent Pikirayi, The Zimbabwe Culture (2001)
Wikipedia: Great Zimbabwe

flows.name: Monsoon dhows between the Swahili coast, Arabia and Gujarat
flows.note: Ships came south from Arabia and India on the northeast monsoon (November-February) and went home on the southwest (April-September), so traders spent months in port; Villiers sailed with a Kuwaiti boom on this circuit in 1938-39. Dhow counts are estimates.

sources.cite: Abdul Sheriff, Dhow Cultures of the Indian Ocean (2010)
Alan Villiers, Sons of Sinbad (1940)
Wikipedia: Swahili coast

flows.name: Tamil merchant guild ships, Nagapattinam to Kedah and China
flows.note: Guilds such as the Ainnurruvar and Manigramam left inscriptions from Sumatra to Quanzhou; the Cholas sent embassies to the Song and raided Srivijaya in 1025. Ship counts are estimates.

sources.cite: Tansen Sen, Buddhism, Diplomacy and Trade (2003)
Noboru Karashima (ed.), Ancient and Medieval Commercial Activities in the Indian Ocean (2002)
Wikipedia: Ainnurruvar

flows.name: Song and Yuan junks, Quanzhou to Calicut
flows.note: Junks left Quanzhou on the winter northeast monsoon and came back in summer; Ibn Battuta saw 13 Chinese junks at Calicut and says the biggest carried 1,000 men, 600 sailors and 400 soldiers. Junk counts are estimates.

sources.cite: Ibn Battuta, Rihla (Gibb and Beckingham, trans., vol. 4)
Zhao Rugua, Zhu fan zhi (1225; F. Hirth and W. W. Rockhill, trans., 1911)
John Chaffee, The Muslim Merchants of Premodern China (2018)

flows.name: Chinese merchant junks between Ningbo and Hakata
flows.note: Private Chinese merchants settled at Hakata and sailed the East China Sea with the summer monsoon; the Shinan wreck (1323) carried 20,000 ceramics and 28 tons of Chinese coin. Ship counts are estimates.

sources.cite: Charlotte von Verschuer, Across the Perilous Sea (2006)
Wikipedia: Shinan shipwreck

flows.name: Hajj caravan from Baghdad and Kufa on the Darb Zubayda
flows.note: Zubayda, wife of Harun al-Rashid, had wells, cisterns and stations built along the 1,400 km road; Ibn Jubayr returned with this caravan in 1184. Party size is an estimate.

sources.cite: Saad al-Rashid, Darb Zubaydah: The Pilgrim Road from Kufa to Mecca (1980)
Ibn Jubayr, Rihla (R. J. C. Broadhurst, trans., 1952)
Wikipedia: Darb Zubaydah

flows.name: Cairo Hajj caravan (the mahmal)
goods_out: the kiswa cloth for the Kaaba
flows.note: From Baybars' time the caravan, led by the amir al-hajj with the mahmal litter, left Cairo in mid-Shawwal and took about 37-40 stages along Sinai and the Hijaz coast; it carried tens of thousands in good years. Party size is an estimate.

sources.cite: Jacques Jomier, Le Mahmal et la caravane égyptienne des pèlerins de la Mecque (1953)
F. E. Peters, The Hajj (1994)
Wikipedia: Mahmal

flows.name: Ottoman Damascus Hajj caravan
flows.note: The governor of Damascus led the caravan, which gathered at Muzayrib and left around mid-Shawwal; it spent about 40 days on the road and was guarded by Ottoman forts and paid-off Bedouin. Pilgrim numbers varied from a few thousand to tens of thousands.

sources.cite: Karl K. Barbir, Ottoman Rule in Damascus, 1708-1758 (1980)
Suraiya Faroqhi, Pilgrims and Sultans: The Hajj under the Ottomans (1990)

flows.name: West African pilgrims overland through the Sudan belt
flows.note: Takrur pilgrims walked east across the savanna, often working on the way for months or years, and crossed the Red Sea from Suakin; many settled in Sudan. Counts and duration are estimates.

sources.cite: J. S. Birks, Across the Savannas to Mecca: The Overland Pilgrimage Route from West Africa (1978)
Umar al-Naqar, The Pilgrimage Tradition in West Africa (1972)

flows.name: Mughal pilgrim and trading ships, Surat to Mocha and Jeddah
flows.note: Surat's big ships sailed for the Red Sea with the northeast monsoon and came back in August-September with the silver that paid for Gujarat's cloth; the emperor's Ganj-i-Sawai, taken by Henry Every in 1695, carried some 600 people. Ship counts follow Das Gupta.

sources.cite: Ashin Das Gupta, Indian Merchants and the Decline of Surat, c. 1700-1750 (1979)
Wikipedia: Ganj-i-Sawai

flows.name: Italian merchants to the Champagne fairs
flows.note: Six fairs a year at Lagny, Bar-sur-Aube, Provins and Troyes drew Italian and Flemish merchants under the Count of Champagne's protection; Sienese couriers covered the road in about three weeks. Group counts are estimates.

sources.cite: Robert-Henri Bautier, 'Les foires de Champagne', Recueils de la Société Jean Bodin 5 (1953)
Richard D. Face, 'Techniques of Business in the Trade between the Fairs of Champagne and the South of Europe', Economic History Review 10 (1958)
Wikipedia: Champagne fairs

flows.name: Hanseatic merchants from Lubeck to Novgorod
flows.note: German merchants lived in the Peterhof in two seasonal groups, summer travellers by sea and winter travellers who came over the ice by sledge; Ivan III closed the Kontor in 1494. Group counts are estimates.

sources.cite: Philippe Dollinger, The German Hansa (1970)
Wikipedia: Peterhof (Novgorod)

flows.name: Hanseatic stockfish trade, Lubeck to Bergen
flows.note: German merchants at the Bryggen Kontor bought dried cod that northern fishermen brought down to Bergen in summer, paying in grain; ship counts are estimates (Bergen customs records of the 1500s list a few hundred ship visits a year).

sources.cite: Philippe Dollinger, The German Hansa (1970)
Arnved Nedkvitne, The German Hansa and Bergen 1100-1600 (2014)
Wikipedia: Bryggen

flows.name: Cogs and hulks between Bruges and the Baltic round Denmark
flows.note: Ships increasingly sailed round Jutland instead of portaging Lubeck-Hamburg; the Sound Toll registers from 1497 record thousands of passages a year by the 1500s. Earlier counts are estimates.

sources.cite: Philippe Dollinger, The German Hansa (1970)
Sound Toll Registers online

flows.name: Genoese galleys and cogs to Pera and Caffa
flows.note: Caffa was Genoa's Black Sea capital from 1266 until the Ottoman conquest of 1475, collecting Crimean grain, steppe goods and slaves; Mamluk Egypt's mamluk soldiers were largely bought here. Ship counts are estimates.

sources.cite: Michel Balard, La Romanie génoise (1978)
Wikipedia: Feodosia (Genoese Caffa)

flows.name: Venetian state galleys to Alexandria (muda)
flows.note: The Senate auctioned the charter of a few great galleys each year, which sailed in convoy in late summer to meet the spice caravans and were back for the Christmas fair; crews of about 200 included oarsmen who traded on their own account.

sources.cite: Frederic C. Lane, Venice: A Maritime Republic (1973), ch. 9
Doris Stöckly, Le système de l'Incanto des galées du marché à Venise (1995)
Wikipedia: Muda (convoy)

flows.name: Venetian state galleys to Beirut (muda of Syria)
flows.note: Sailed with the Alexandria galleys as far as Crete or Cyprus, then to Beirut, the port of Damascus, where the autumn spice caravans arrived.

sources.cite: Frederic C. Lane, Venice: A Maritime Republic (1973)
Eliyahu Ashtor, Levant Trade in the Later Middle Ages (1983)

flows.name: Venetian galleys of Flanders to Southampton and Bruges
flows.note: From 1314, regularly from the 1370s, three to five great galleys left in spring, wintered in England or Flanders and returned the next year; the voyage out took two to three months.

sources.cite: Frederic C. Lane, Venice: A Maritime Republic (1973)
Alwyn A. Ruddock, Italian Merchants and Shipping in Southampton, 1270-1600 (1951)

flows.name: Venetian galleys of Romania to Constantinople and Tana
flows.note: Galleys sailed in midsummer to Constantinople, then on to Tana at the mouth of the Don and Trebizond for goods from Tabriz and the steppe; the route faded with the Ottoman conquests.

sources.cite: Frederic C. Lane, Venice: A Maritime Republic (1973)
Freddy Thiriet, La Romanie vénitienne au Moyen Âge (1959)

flows.name: Pilgrim galleys from Venice to Jaffa
flows.note: Private patrons licensed by the state left after Ascension with a hundred or so pilgrims; Felix Fabri's 1483 galley left Venice on 1 June and reached Jaffa on 1 July, and the round trip including the Holy Land tour took about four months.

sources.cite: Felix Fabri, Evagatorium (1484)
H. F. M. Prescott, Jerusalem Journey: Pilgrimage to the Holy Land in the Fifteenth Century (1954)

flows.name: Pilgrims on the Camino de Santiago from Paris
flows.note: The twelfth-century Pilgrim's Guide in the Codex Calixtinus gives the four French roads and the stages beyond the Pyrenees; pilgrims walked in small bands, mostly in spring and summer, to arrive for St James's day (25 July). Numbers are estimates.

sources.cite: Codex Calixtinus, Book V (Pilgrim's Guide), c. 1140 (William Melczer, trans., 1993)
Wikipedia: Camino de Santiago

flows.name: Crusader and pilgrim passages from Marseille to Acre
flows.note: Ships ran to the crusader ports twice a year, the spring passage around Easter and the summer passage in August; Marseille's 1253-55 statutes limited pilgrim loads. Counts are estimates.

sources.cite: John H. Pryor, Geography, Technology and War (1988)
Wikipedia: Passagium generale

flows.name: Students travelling to Bologna and Paris
flows.note: Students from across Latin Europe studied law at Bologna and theology at Paris, organised in 'nations'; Bologna's German nation matriculated dozens a year. They travelled in small groups before the academic year. Counts are estimates.

sources.cite: Hilde de Ridder-Symoens (ed.), A History of the University in Europe, vol. 1 (1992)
Wikipedia: Medieval university

flows.name: Merchants on the Mongol road from Tana to Cathay (Pegolotti)
flows.note: Pegolotti's handbook gives the legs: Tana to Astrakhan 25 days by ox-wagon, Sarai to Saraichuk 8, to Urgench 20 by camel, to Otrar 35-40, to Almaliq 45 by donkey, to Ganzhou 70, then 45 to the river and on to Khanbaliq; 'the road is perfectly safe by day and night'. Group counts are estimates.

sources.cite: Francesco Balducci Pegolotti, La pratica della mercatura (c. 1340), in Henry Yule, Cathay and the Way Thither, vol. 3 (1914)
Wikipedia: Francesco Balducci Pegolotti

flows.name: Mongol yam relay riders, Khanbaliq to Karakorum and Tabriz
flows.note: Ögedei set up the yam in 1235; Marco Polo describes stations every 25-30 miles with hundreds of horses each, and express riders covering 200-250 miles a day in emergencies. End-to-end time and counts are estimates.

sources.cite: Marco Polo, The Description of the World, book 2 (A. C. Moule and P. Pelliot, trans., 1938)
Adam J. Silverstein, Postal Systems in the Pre-Modern Islamic World (2007), ch. 4
Wikipedia: Yam (route)

flows.name: Ming treasure fleets of Zheng He
flows.note: Seven voyages in 28 years, each with about 250 ships and up to 27,800 men; they gathered at Changle and sailed on the winter monsoon, returning in summer. per_year is the average rate of whole fleets, party the whole fleet.

sources.cite: Edward L. Dreyer, Zheng He: China and the Oceans in the Early Ming Dynasty, 1405-1433 (2007)
Ma Huan, Yingya Shenglan (1433)
Wikipedia: Treasure voyages

flows.name: Joseon tribute embassies to Beijing
flows.note: Joseon sent regular embassies three or four times a year (New Year, the emperor's birthday, the solstice) plus special ones; diaries such as Pak Chiwon's Yeolha Ilgi (1780) record parties of about 250 and roughly 50 days each way.

sources.cite: Pak Chiwon, Yeolha Ilgi (1780)
Wikipedia: Joseon missions to Imperial China

flows.name: Ryukyu tribute ships to Fuzhou
flows.note: Ryukyu was the most frequent Ming tributary (171 missions recorded in the Ming annals), first yearly and later every two years; ships sailed for Fuzhou in autumn and envoys went overland to Beijing. Ship counts per year are estimates.

sources.cite: Gregory Smits, Visions of Ryukyu (1999)
Wikipedia: Ryukyu Kingdom

flows.name: Japanese tally-trade missions to Ming (kango boeki)
flows.note: Seventeen official missions of up to ten ships sailed under Ming tallies, landing at Ningbo; the 1523 Ningbo incident between rival Hosokawa and Ouchi missions nearly ended them. per_year is ships per year averaged.

sources.cite: Charlotte von Verschuer, Across the Perilous Sea (2006)
Wikipedia: Japanese missions to Ming China

flows.name: Examination candidates travelling to the capital
flows.note: Every three years thousands of provincial graduates (juren) travelled to the metropolitan exam held in Beijing in spring, often by Grand Canal boat; the Ming and Qing admitted roughly 200-400 jinshi per session from about 5,000-10,000 candidates. per_year averages one session in three.

sources.cite: Benjamin A. Elman, A Cultural History of Civil Examinations in Late Imperial China (2000)
Wikipedia: Imperial examination

flows.name: Ming tribute grain barges on the Grand Canal
goods_out: tax rice (about 4 million shi a year)
flows.note: From 1415 all tax grain for Beijing went by canal: Ray Huang counts 11,775 boats crewed by about 120,000 soldiers, leaving the Yangzi in early spring to reach Tongzhou by summer.

sources.cite: Ray Huang, Taxation and Governmental Finance in Sixteenth-Century Ming China (1974)
Ray Huang, 'The Grand Canal during the Ming Dynasty' (PhD thesis, 1964)
Wikipedia: Grand Canal (China)

flows.name: Qing tribute grain barges on the Grand Canal
flows.note: The Qing kept about 6,000-7,000 grain junks on the canal, crewed by hired boatmen whose brotherhoods became the Green Gang; the Yellow River's shift in 1855 cut the canal and shipping moved to sea.

sources.cite: Jane Kate Leonard, Controlling from Afar: The Daoguang Emperor's Management of the Grand Canal Crisis (1996)
Wikipedia: Grand Canal (China)

flows.name: Tea-horse caravans from Sichuan to Lhasa
flows.note: The Song set up a Tea and Horse Agency in 1074 to buy war horses with Sichuan tea; porters carried tea bricks up to Kangding and yak and mule trains took them over the passes to Lhasa, a trip of several months. Caravan counts are estimates.

sources.cite: Paul J. Smith, Taxing Heaven's Storehouse: Horses, Bureaucrats and the Destruction of the Sichuan Tea Industry 1074-1224 (1991)
Wikipedia: Tea Horse Road

flows.name: Pilgrims to the Magh Mela and Kumbh at Prayag
flows.note: Xuanzang described a great bathing gathering at Prayag under Harsha in 643; the annual Magh Mela in January-February swells every twelfth year into the Kumbh, with millions of pilgrims by the 19th century. Group counts are estimates, and pilgrims came from all over India (the stops are one feeder route).

sources.cite: Kama Maclean, Pilgrimage and Power: The Kumbh Mela in Allahabad, 1765-1954 (2008)
Wikipedia: Kumbh Mela

flows.name: Banjara pack-bullock caravans
flows.note: Banjara clans moved grain and salt on pack oxen in herds of thousands, supplying Mughal and later British armies; Tavernier saw caravans of 10,000-12,000 oxen. They travelled in the dry season. Counts are estimates.

sources.cite: Jean-Baptiste Tavernier, Travels in India (1676; V. Ball, trans., 1889), book 1 ch. 3
Wikipedia: Banjara

flows.name: Great desert caravan, Aleppo to Basra
flows.note: Large caravans of up to several thousand camels crossed the Syrian desert with Bedouin escorts, taking 40-70 days; travellers' accounts from Teixeira (1605) to the 1750s are collected by Carruthers. Caravan counts are estimates.

sources.cite: Douglas Carruthers (ed.), The Desert Route to India (Hakluyt Society, 1929)

flows.name: Armenian New Julfa merchants, Isfahan to Bandar Abbas and Surat
flows.note: Shah Abbas resettled Armenians at New Julfa in 1605 and they ran a network from Amsterdam to Manila; the commenda account book of Hovhannes Joughayetsi (1682-93) records his journeys. Counts are estimates.

sources.cite: Sebouh David Aslanian, From the Indian Ocean to the Mediterranean: The Global Trade Networks of Armenian Merchants from New Julfa (2011)

flows.name: Ottoman ulak couriers on the imperial road to Baghdad
flows.note: Couriers (ulak) changed horses at menzil stations on the 'right arm' road through Anatolia to Syria and Iraq; ordinary travel took months, express couriers a few weeks. Times and counts are estimates.

sources.cite: Colin Heywood, 'The Ottoman Menzilhane and Ulak System in Rumeli in the Eighteenth Century' (1980)
Yusuf Halaçoğlu, Osmanlılarda Ulaşım ve Haberleşme (Menziller) (2002)

flows.name: Ottoman campaign armies marching from Istanbul to Hungary
flows.note: The army left Istanbul in spring and needed two to three months on the military road to reach Hungary, leaving a short fighting season; Murphey reconstructs marching rates from campaign diaries. Counts are estimates.

sources.cite: Rhoads Murphey, Ottoman Warfare, 1500-1700 (1999)

flows.name: Spanish infantry on the Spanish Road, Milan to Flanders
flows.note: Geoffrey Parker counts some 123,000 men marching up the corridor in 1567-1620, typically taking about 40 days for the thousand kilometres from Milan to Namur; a tercio of 3,000 is a typical group.

sources.cite: Geoffrey Parker, The Army of Flanders and the Spanish Road, 1567-1659 (1972)
Wikipedia: Spanish Road

flows.name: Portuguese India fleet, Lisbon to Goa (Carreira da India)
flows.note: Ships left Lisbon in March-April to round the Cape in time for the monsoon and reach Goa in September; they sailed back from Goa in December-January. Between 1500 and 1635 about 900 ships sailed out, and the big naus of 1600 carried 600-800 people.

sources.cite: C. R. Boxer, The Portuguese Seaborne Empire (1969)
A. R. Disney, A History of Portugal and the Portuguese Empire, vol. 2 (2009)
Wikipedia: Portuguese India Armadas

flows.name: Spanish treasure fleet to Veracruz (flota de Nueva España)
flows.note: The New Spain flota left Andalusia in spring and wintered at Veracruz while the trade fair at Jalapa ran; it joined the Tierra Firme galleons at Havana and sailed home through the Florida Strait. Ship counts and voyage times follow Chaunu's series.

sources.cite: Huguette and Pierre Chaunu, Séville et l'Atlantique 1504-1650 (1955-59)
Wikipedia: Spanish treasure fleet

flows.name: Spanish galleons of Tierra Firme to Cartagena and Portobelo
flows.note: The galleons sailed in late summer to Cartagena and the Portobelo fair, where Peruvian silver came over the isthmus from Panama; they met the New Spain fleet at Havana for the return. Counts follow Chaunu.

sources.cite: Huguette and Pierre Chaunu, Séville et l'Atlantique 1504-1650 (1955-59)
Wikipedia: Spanish treasure fleet

flows.name: Manila galleons, Manila to Acapulco
flows.note: One or two galleons a year left Cavite in late June or July, ran north to catch the westerlies, and reached Acapulco four to six months later; the return on the trade winds by Guam took about three months. Crews were largely Filipino.

sources.cite: William Lytle Schurz, The Manila Galleon (1939)
Glyn Williams, The Prize of All the Oceans (1999)
Wikipedia: Manila galleon

flows.name: Dutch East India Company ships, Texel to Batavia (summary)
flows.note: Summary only: the real voyages come from the Dutch-Asiatic Shipping dataset. About 4,700 outward voyages left in three fleets a year (Christmas, Easter, fair-time); return fleets left Batavia around December-January. The voyage out took about eight months.

sources.cite: J. R. Bruijn, F. S. Gaastra and I. Schöffer, Dutch-Asiatic Shipping in the 17th and 18th Centuries (1979-87)

flows.name: English East India Company ships, London to Madras, Bombay and Canton
flows.note: East Indiamen left the Downs early in the year to catch the monsoon and spent about six months outward; by the late 18th century some 30-50 a year sailed. Counts follow Farrington's register.

sources.cite: Anthony Farrington, Catalogue of East India Company Ships' Journals and Logs 1600-1834 (1999)
Wikipedia: East Indiaman

flows.name: Japanese red-seal ships to Southeast Asia (shuinsen)
flows.note: The shogunate licensed about 356 voyages between 1604 and 1635, roughly 11 a year, before the seclusion edicts; ships of 200-300 men sailed south on the winter monsoon.

sources.cite: Iwao Seiichi, Shuinsen boekishi no kenkyu (1958)
Wikipedia: Red seal ships

flows.name: Chinese junks to Nagasaki
flows.note: Chinese junks were the main channel of Edo Japan's foreign trade; arrivals peaked near 190 in 1688, then the 1715 Shotoku regulations cut licences to 30 a year. Crews lived in the Tojin yashiki compound.

sources.cite: Robert LeRoy Innes, 'The Door Ajar: Japan's Foreign Trade in the Seventeenth Century' (PhD, 1980)
Wikipedia: Sakoku

flows.name: Makassan trepang fleets to Marege (Arnhem Land)
flows.note: Each December fleets of 30-60 praus with about 1,000 men sailed with the northwest monsoon to the Australian coast to boil and dry sea cucumber for the China market, staying until the southeast winds took them home in April; Yolngu people traded and some sailed with them.

sources.cite: C. C. Macknight, The Voyage to Marege: Macassan Trepangers in Northern Australia (1976)
Wikipedia: Makassan contact with Australia

flows.name: Slave ships from the Bight of Benin to Bahia
flows.note: Bahian ships bartered tobacco for captives at Ouidah and the Slave Coast; about 1.1 million people were carried from the Bight of Benin to Bahia. The party is the people held aboard (about 380) plus a crew of about 30; render them as people, each with a name and a home.

sources.cite: Slave Voyages: Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database
Pierre Verger, Trade Relations between the Bight of Benin and Bahia (1976)

flows.dignity: Generated people here were enslaved. Give them names, origins and fates; never list them as goods.

flows.name: Slave ships from Luanda and Benguela to Rio de Janeiro
flows.note: West Central Africa was the largest source of the trade; Brazilian ships made the crossing in about five weeks and carried over two million people to Rio and its region. The party is the people held aboard plus about 30 crew.

sources.cite: Slave Voyages: Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database
Joseph C. Miller, Way of Death: Merchant Capitalism and the Angolan Slave Trade, 1730-1830 (1988)

flows.dignity: Generated people here were enslaved. Give them names, origins and fates; never list them as goods.

flows.name: British slave voyages: Liverpool, Bonny, Jamaica
flows.note: Liverpool ships traded at Bonny and Old Calabar for months, then crossed to the Caribbean in about two months; in the 1790s Liverpool sent over 100 voyages a year. Mortality on the passage averaged around 12-15 per cent. The party is the people held aboard plus about 35 crew; Olaudah Equiano's account describes the passage.

sources.cite: Slave Voyages: Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database
Olaudah Equiano, The Interesting Narrative of the Life of Olaudah Equiano (1789)
Marcus Rediker, The Slave Ship: A Human History (2007)

flows.dignity: Generated people here were enslaved. Give them names, origins and fates; never list them as goods.

flows.name: Indian indentured labourers, Calcutta to Mauritius and Trinidad
flows.note: After abolition about 1.3 million Indians signed indentures for the sugar colonies; sailing ships from the Calcutta depots took about two months to Mauritius and three to the Caribbean, and departures were restricted to the cooler months. Counts are averages.

sources.cite: Hugh Tinker, A New System of Slavery: The Export of Indian Labour Overseas, 1830-1920 (1974)
Wikipedia: Indian indenture system

flows.name: Inca chasqui relay runners, Cusco to Quito
goods_out: light goods for the Sapa Inca
flows.note: Runners posted in pairs at huts every few kilometres along the Qhapaq Nan passed messages and khipu at a sprint; chroniclers claim Cusco-Quito, about 2,000 km, in under two weeks. Time and frequency are estimates.

sources.cite: John Hyslop, The Inka Road System (1984)
Bernabé Cobo, History of the Inca Empire (1653; R. Hamilton, trans., 1979)
Wikipedia: Chasqui

flows.name: Llama caravans between Cusco and the Titicaca basin
flows.note: Herders drove llama trains of a few dozen animals, each carrying 25-30 kg about 20 km a day, swapping highland and valley products in the dry season; the practice survived into the 20th century. Counts are estimates.

sources.cite: John V. Murra, The Economic Organization of the Inka State (1980)
Henry Browman, 'La trashumancia precolombina en los Andes' (1974)

flows.name: Mita labour drafts walking to Potosi
flows.note: Viceroy Toledo's mita required 16 highland provinces to send about 13,500 men a year to the silver mines; they walked with families and llamas for up to two months, and many never returned home. party is a provincial contingent.

sources.cite: Peter Bakewell, Miners of the Red Mountain: Indian Labor in Potosí, 1545-1650 (1984)
Jeffrey A. Cole, The Potosí Mita, 1573-1700 (1985)
Wikipedia: Mit'a

flows.name: Aztec pochteca long-distance merchants
flows.note: Sahagún's informants describe pochteca caravans leaving Tlatelolco on an auspicious day sign, travelling by night with tlameme porters each carrying about 23 kg, and doubling as spies; numbers and timing are estimates.

sources.cite: Bernardino de Sahagún, Florentine Codex, book 9 (A. J. O. Anderson and C. Dibble, trans., 1959)
Wikipedia: Pochteca

flows.name: Maya trading canoes around Yucatan
flows.note: In 1502 Columbus's men met off Guanaja a Maya trading canoe 'as long as a galley', eight feet wide, with about 25 rowers and cargo of cloth, copper, obsidian swords and cacao; counts are estimates.

sources.cite: Ferdinand Columbus, The Life of the Admiral Christopher Columbus (1571), ch. 89
Anthony P. Andrews, Maya Salt Production and Trade (1983)

flows.name: Hopewell exchange journeys to Ohio ceremonial centres
flows.note: Ohio Hopewell earthworks hold Yellowstone obsidian, Lake Superior copper, Appalachian mica and Gulf shell; whether by traders, pilgrims or relays is debated. Everything here is a rough order of magnitude.

sources.cite: Bradley T. Lepper, Ohio Archaeology (2005)
Wikipedia: Hopewell tradition

flows.name: Mississippian river canoes to Cahokia
flows.note: Cahokia's population of perhaps 10,000-20,000 drew goods by dugout along the Mississippi system; Mill Creek hoes and Gulf shell spread across the Southeast. Counts are rough orders of magnitude.

sources.cite: Timothy R. Pauketat, Cahokia: Ancient America's Great City on the Mississippi (2009)
Wikipedia: Cahokia

flows.name: Hudson's Bay Company ships, London to York Factory
flows.note: Two or three ships sailed each June, often recruiting Orkneymen at Stromness, and reached the Bay in August when the ice allowed; they had to leave by September. Counts are attested in the Company's archives.

sources.cite: E. E. Rich, The History of the Hudson's Bay Company, 1670-1870 (1958-59)
Wikipedia: York Factory

flows.name: North West Company voyageur brigades, Montreal to Grand Portage
flows.note: Each May canots de maître of 8-10 paddlers left Lachine, paddling 14-16 hours a day and portaging packs of 40 kg, to reach the rendezvous at Grand Portage (later Fort William) in about seven or eight weeks and return before freeze-up.

sources.cite: Grace Lee Nute, The Voyageur (1931)
Carolyn Podruchny, Making the Voyageur World (2006)
Wikipedia: Voyageurs

flows.name: Santa Fe Trail wagon caravans
flows.note: Josiah Gregg tallied the yearly trade: in 1831 some 130 wagons and 320 men went out; caravans formed at Council Grove and took about seven or eight weeks. Counts vary widely by year.

sources.cite: Josiah Gregg, Commerce of the Prairies (1844)
Wikipedia: Santa Fe Trail

flows.name: Oregon and California Trail emigrant wagon trains
flows.note: About 400,000 people went west on the trails between 1841 and the railroad in 1869, leaving the Missouri in late April or May as the grass came up and taking four to six months; companies of 20-60 wagons were typical. Emigration peaked in the 1849-52 gold rush.

sources.cite: John D. Unruh, The Plains Across: The Overland Emigrants and the Trans-Mississippi West, 1840-60 (1979)
Wikipedia: Oregon Trail

flows.name: Russian promyshlenniki fur parties across Siberia
flows.note: Bands of hunters and traders went by river and portage, wintering in ostrogs, to take sable themselves or collect yasak from Siberian peoples; Yakutsk was reached in 1632. A journey east often took more than a year. Counts are estimates.

sources.cite: Raymond H. Fisher, The Russian Fur Trade, 1550-1700 (1943)
Janet Martin, Treasure of the Land of Darkness (1986)

flows.name: Kyakhta tea caravans from Kalgan across Mongolia
flows.note: After the Treaty of Kyakhta (1727) all Russo-Chinese trade went through one border market; Shanxi merchants sent tea by camel across the Gobi in the cool season, about 40 days from Kalgan. Caravan counts are estimates.

sources.cite: Clifford M. Foust, Muscovite and Mandarin: Russia's Trade with China and its Setting, 1727-1805 (1969)
Wikipedia: Kyakhta trade

flows.name: Bukharan caravans to Orenburg
flows.note: Caravans of up to a few thousand camels crossed the Kazakh steppe to the Orenburg exchange; nineteenth-century Russian accounts give about two to three months. Counts are estimates.

sources.cite: Audrey Burton, The Bukharans: A Dynastic, Diplomatic and Commercial History, 1550-1702 (1997)
Wikipedia: Orenburg

flows.name: Polynesian voyaging canoes between Tahiti and Hawaii
flows.note: Hawaiian tradition remembers two-way voyages in the voyaging era, and Hokule'a's 1976 replica voyage from Hawaii to Tahiti took 33 days without instruments; frequency and timing are rough estimates.

sources.cite: Ben Finney, Voyage of Rediscovery (1994)
Patrick V. Kirch, On the Road of the Winds (2000)
Wikipedia: Polynesian navigation

flows.name: Tongan voyages to Samoa and Fiji
flows.note: Tongan chiefs kept ties of marriage and tribute with Samoa and Fiji, and Tongans built big double canoes (kalia) from Lau timber; Cook and Mariner (1806-10) describe frequent crossings. Counts are estimates.

sources.cite: William Mariner and John Martin, An Account of the Natives of the Tonga Islands (1817)
Patrick V. Kirch, The Evolution of the Polynesian Chiefdoms (1984)

flows.name: Kula expeditions in the Massim (Trobriands to Dobu)
flows.note: Malinowski described fleets of decorated canoes sailing to exchange necklaces clockwise and armbands anticlockwise round the island ring; a big uvalaku expedition of dozens of canoes from Sinaketa reached Dobu in a few days. Start date is approximate (the ring is at least several centuries old).

sources.cite: Bronisław Malinowski, Argonauts of the Western Pacific (1922)
Wikipedia: Kula ring

flows.name: Mesta sheep drives between Leon and Extremadura
flows.note: Alfonso X chartered the Mesta in 1273; by the 1500s some 2-3 million merino sheep walked the cañadas reales south in autumn and back north in April-May, flocks of about 1,000 led by shepherds and dogs. Klein gives the organisation and numbers.

sources.cite: Julius Klein, The Mesta: A Study in Spanish Economic History, 1273-1836 (1920)
Wikipedia: Mesta

flows.name: Bakhtiari seasonal migration over the Zagros
flows.note: Whole Bakhtiari tribes move up to summer pastures in spring and down in autumn, swimming flocks across the Karun on inflated skins; the 1925 film Grass followed one migration of about 50,000 people over 46 days. Group counts are estimates.

sources.cite: Merian C. Cooper, Grass: A Nation's Battle for Life (1925)
Gene R. Garthwaite, Khans and Shahs: A History of the Bakhtiyari Tribe in Iran (1983)
Wikipedia: Bakhtiari people

flows.name: Rwala Bedouin camel migration, Nafud to the Syrian steppe
flows.note: Alois Musil lived with the Rwala in 1908-15 and describes them wintering in the Nafud and moving north in late spring to wells and markets near the Syrian sown land, returning south in autumn. Group counts are estimates.

sources.cite: Alois Musil, The Manners and Customs of the Rwala Bedouins (1928)
Wikipedia: Rwala

flows.name: Maasai herders moving cattle between dry and wet season pastures

stops.name: Rift Valley floor (dry-season grazing near Lake Natron)

flows.note: Maasai age-sets of young men (ilmurran) took herds to distant wet-season grasslands and back to permanent water in the dry season; distances and group sizes here are rough orders of magnitude.

sources.cite: Dorothy L. Hodgson, Once Intrepid Warriors (2001)
Wikipedia: Maasai people

flows.name: Sami reindeer migration to the Norwegian coast
flows.note: Reindeer-herding siida families move herds from inland winter pastures to coastal islands for calving and summer, swimming them across sounds, and back in autumn. Group counts are estimates.

sources.cite: Hugh Beach, A Year in Lapland (1993)
Wikipedia: Reindeer herding

flows.name: Fulani cattle transhumance in the inner Niger delta
flows.note: Seku Amadu's Masina state (1818) fixed the dates and routes by which herds re-entered the flooded delta pastures (the bourgou) as the water fell, crossing the river at set points; group counts are estimates.

sources.cite: Jean Gallais, Le Delta intérieur du Niger (1967)
Wikipedia: Massina Empire

flows.name: Daimyo processions on the Tokaido (sankin-kotai)
flows.note: From 1635 daimyo spent alternate years in Edo, travelling in processions of a few hundred to several thousand retainers, mostly in the fourth month; the Tokaido's 53 stations took about two weeks from Kyoto. Per-year counts on this road are estimates.

sources.cite: Constantine N. Vaporis, Tour of Duty: Samurai, Military Service in Edo, and the Culture of Early Modern Japan (2008)
Wikipedia: Sankin-kōtai

flows.name: Pilgrims to the Ise shrines (Ise mairi)
goods_out: travel money from a pilgrimage confraternity (ko)
flows.note: Villages pooled money in Ise-ko confraternities and sent members in turn; perhaps 400,000 pilgrims came in an ordinary year, and in the okage mairi surges of 1705, 1771 and 1830 several million went in a few months. Groups and size are estimates.

sources.cite: Winston Davis, 'Pilgrimage and World Renewal' in Japanese Religion and Society (1992)
Wikipedia: Ise Grand Shrine

flows.name: Dutch ships from Batavia to Dejima
flows.note: From 1641 the VOC alone among Europeans traded at Nagasaki: ships left Batavia in June on the southwest monsoon and returned in November; the number fell from several a year to one or two by the 1790s. The Dutch chief made a court journey to Edo each spring (yearly until 1790).

sources.cite: Leonard Blussé et al. (eds), The Deshima Dagregisters (1986-)
Wikipedia: Dejima

flows.name: Grand Tour travellers from London to Rome and Naples
flows.note: Young gentlemen spent one to three years abroad with a tutor; they typically crossed the Alps in autumn to winter in Rome, spent Holy Week there and went south to Naples. Counts are estimates (Ingamells' dictionary lists about 6,000 British travellers to Italy, 1701-1800).

sources.cite: Jeremy Black, The British Abroad: The Grand Tour in the Eighteenth Century (1992)
John Ingamells, A Dictionary of British and Irish Travellers in Italy, 1701-1800 (1997)
Wikipedia: Grand Tour

flows.name: Atlantic sailing packets, New York to Liverpool (Black Ball Line)
flows.note: The Black Ball Line began the first fixed-date sailings in January 1818, at first monthly, then twice a month; its packets averaged 23 days eastward and 40 days westward against the wind.

sources.cite: Robert G. Albion, Square-Riggers on Schedule: The New York Sail Packets to England, France and the Cotton Ports (1938)
Wikipedia: Black Ball Line (trans-Atlantic packet)

flows.name: Clipper ships, New York to San Francisco round Cape Horn
flows.note: The gold rush filled the clippers; average passages were about 120 days and Flying Cloud made it in 89 days in 1851 and 1854. Counts are estimates from San Francisco arrivals.

sources.cite: Carl C. Cutler, Greyhounds of the Sea: The Story of the American Clipper Ship (1930)
Wikipedia: Flying Cloud (clipper)

flows.name: Tea clippers, Fuzhou to London
flows.note: Clippers raced to bring the new season's tea from Fuzhou; in the Great Tea Race of 1866 Ariel, Taeping and Serica left the Min River together on 30 May and docked in London 99 days later. The Suez Canal and steam ended the trade.

sources.cite: Basil Lubbock, The China Clippers (1914)
Wikipedia: Great Tea Race of 1866

flows.name: Pony Express riders, St Joseph to Sacramento
flows.note: From April 1860 to October 1861 riders changing horses at about 190 stations carried mail the 1,900 miles in about ten days, weekly then twice weekly, until the transcontinental telegraph made it obsolete.

sources.cite: Raymond W. Settle and Mary L. Settle, Saddles and Spurs: The Pony Express Saga (1955)
Wikipedia: Pony Express

flows.name: Overland Route mail and passengers, Southampton to Bombay via Egypt
goods_out: officials and officers of the Indian services
flows.note: P&O steamers carried the India mail to Alexandria, passengers crossed Egypt by canal boat, Nile steamer and desert van to Suez, and another steamer ran on to Bombay; the journey shrank from about four months round the Cape to about a month.

sources.cite: Freda Harcourt, Flagships of Imperialism: The P&O Company and the Politics of Empire (2006)
Wikipedia: Overland route

flows.name: Emigrant steamers, Liverpool to New York
flows.note: Cunard, Inman and White Star liners called at Queenstown for Irish emigrants; crossings fell from about two weeks in the 1850s to about a week by 1900, and steerage carried most of the more than 4 million who sailed from Liverpool. Ship counts are estimates.

sources.cite: Drew Keeling, The Business of Transatlantic Migration between Europe and the United States, 1900-1914 (2012)
Wikipedia: Ellis Island

flows.name: Emigrant steamers, Hamburg and Bremen to New York
goods_out: German, Polish, Jewish and Russian emigrants
flows.note: HAPAG and Norddeutscher Lloyd carried most Central and Eastern European emigrants, whom Hamburg housed in its Ballinstadt halls before sailing; about a third of all migrants to the US in 1900-14 left from these two ports. Ship counts are estimates.

sources.cite: Drew Keeling, The Business of Transatlantic Migration (2012)
Wikipedia: BallinStadt

flows.name: Emigrant steamers, Naples and Genoa to New York and Buenos Aires
flows.note: About 4 million Italians went to the US and 2 million to Argentina in 1880-1914, many as seasonal 'golondrinas'; Naples-New York took about two weeks. An alternate destination for each ship is Buenos Aires (about three weeks). Ship counts are estimates.

sources.cite: Donna R. Gabaccia, Italy's Many Diasporas (2000)
Wikipedia: Italian diaspora

flows.name: Chinese emigrants by steamer, Hong Kong to San Francisco
goods_back: remains of the dead for burial at home
flows.note: Pacific Mail's monthly, later twice-monthly, steamers took Taishanese and other Cantonese men to the gold fields and railroads; about 100,000 came before the Exclusion Act of 1882 stopped most immigration.

sources.cite: Elizabeth Sinn, Pacific Crossing: California Gold, Chinese Migration, and the Making of Hong Kong (2013)
Wikipedia: Chinese Exclusion Act

flows.name: Nyamwezi and Swahili ivory caravans, Bagamoyo to Ujiji
flows.note: Caravans of hundreds of porters, many Nyamwezi professionals carrying 30-35 kg tusks, walked the central route in the dry season; Burton and Speke went with one in 1857 and took about four and a half months to Ujiji. Counts are estimates.

sources.cite: Stephen J. Rockel, Carriers of Culture: Labor on the Road in Nineteenth-Century East Africa (2006)
Richard F. Burton, The Lake Regions of Central Africa (1860)

flows.name: Union-Castle mail steamers, Southampton to Cape Town
flows.note: The Union Line's mail contract of 1857 began monthly sailings of about 42 days; by 1900 the weekly mail ships ran Southampton-Madeira-Cape Town in about 17 days, leaving every Thursday afternoon at 4.

sources.cite: Marischal Murray, Union-Castle Chronicle 1853-1953 (1953)
Wikipedia: Union-Castle Line

flows.name: Steamers through the Suez Canal to Bombay
flows.note: After 1869 London-Bombay by P&O and its rivals fell to about three weeks; the canal handled 486 ships in 1870 and over 3,000 a year by 1885. per_year here counts passenger liners on the India run (estimated).

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Suez Canal
Freda Harcourt, Flagships of Imperialism (2006)

flows.name: Hejaz Railway pilgrim trains, Damascus to Medina
flows.note: The railway reached Medina in 1908 and cut the 40-day caravan trip to about five days; it carried tens of thousands of pilgrims a year until T. E. Lawrence and the Arab Revolt wrecked the line in 1916-18. Train counts are estimates.

sources.cite: William Ochsenwald, The Hijaz Railroad (1980)
Wikipedia: Hejaz railway

flows.name: Settler trains on the Trans-Siberian Railway
flows.note: About 4 million peasants moved east to Siberia in 1896-1914, peaking with the Stolypin reforms in 1907-09; they rode slow 'teplushka' freight cars and were registered at the Chelyabinsk resettlement point. Train counts are estimates.

sources.cite: Donald W. Treadgold, The Great Siberian Migration (1957)
Wikipedia: Trans-Siberian Railway

flows.name: Trans-Siberian express, Moscow to Vladivostok
flows.note: With the Chinese Eastern Railway open across Manchuria, the weekly, later twice-weekly, international express took about ten days from Moscow, making London to Tokyo two weeks faster than by sea.

sources.cite: Harmon Tupper, To the Great Ocean: Siberia and the Trans-Siberian Railway (1965)
Wikipedia: Trans-Siberian Railway

flows.name: Imperial Airways airmail, London to Karachi
flows.note: The weekly service opened on 30 March 1929 and took seven days, with the Paris-Basle leg by rail at first; it was later extended to Calcutta, Singapore and, with Qantas, Brisbane (1935).

sources.cite: Robin Higham, Britain's Imperial Air Routes, 1918 to 1939 (1960)
Wikipedia: Imperial Airways

flows.name: Pan Am flying boats across the Pacific
flows.note: The China Clipper opened the San Francisco-Manila airmail in November 1935, flying by day and staying overnight on the islands; the trip took about six days. Weekly service is the documented rate.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: China Clipper
Robert L. Gandt, China Clipper: The Age of the Great Flying Boats (1991)

flows.name: Kilwa coasting ships to Sofala
flows.note: Kilwa's sultans controlled the gold coming down to Sofala, and its copper coins and Great Mosque show the wealth; ships went south with the northeast monsoon. Counts are estimates.

sources.cite: Neville Chittick, Kilwa: An Islamic Trading City on the East African Coast (1974)
Wikipedia: Kilwa Sultanate

flows.name: Karimi spice merchants, Aden to Cairo
flows.note: Karimi merchant houses sailed spices up the Red Sea to Aydhab, carried them by camel 12-15 days to Qus on the Nile and floated them down to Fustat; Ibn Battuta and the Geniza letters describe the route. Counts are estimates.

sources.cite: S. D. Goitein, A Mediterranean Society (1967-88) and Letters of Medieval Jewish Traders (1973)
Eliyahu Ashtor, 'The Karimi Merchants', Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society (1956)
Wikipedia: Aidhab

flows.name: Gujarati ships to Malacca
flows.note: Tomé Pires (1512-15) says four big Gujarati ships came to Malacca each year, a thousand Gujarati merchants lived there and four or five thousand Gujarati sailors came and went; cloth from Cambay was the main import.

sources.cite: Tomé Pires, Suma Oriental (1512-15; Armando Cortesão, trans., 1944)
Wikipedia: Malacca Sultanate

flows.name: Srivijayan and Javanese envoys to the Tang and Song courts
flows.note: Chinese annals record dozens of Srivijayan missions (about 20 to the Song alone); envoys sailed with the southwest monsoon to Guangzhou and went overland to the capital. Group counts are approximate averages.

sources.cite: O. W. Wolters, Early Indonesian Commerce: A Study of the Origins of Srivijaya (1967)
Wikipedia: Srivijaya

flows.name: Chinese traders to Angkor (Zhou Daguan's route)
flows.note: Zhou Daguan left Wenzhou in February 1296 and reached Angkor via Champa, the Mekong and the Tonle Sap by about August; he lists what Chinese traders sold and bought there. Counts are estimates.

sources.cite: Zhou Daguan, A Record of Cambodia: The Land and Its People (Peter Harris, trans., 2007)

flows.name: Ladakhi caravans, Leh to Yarkand and Lhasa
flows.note: The 1684 Treaty of Tingmosgang tied Ladakh's wool trade to Kashmir, and summer caravans crossed the Karakoram, the highest trade route in the world, to Yarkand; British trade reports of the 1870s count hundreds of animals a year. Counts are estimates.

sources.cite: Janet Rizvi, Trans-Himalayan Caravans: Merchant Princes and Peasant Traders in Ladakh (1999)

flows.name: Hokkien junks from Yuegang to Manila
flows.note: When the Ming lifted the sea ban in 1567, junks from Yuegang carried the silk the Manila galleons took to Acapulco; arrivals of 30-50 a year are recorded in Manila's customs (almojarifazgo) in the decades around 1600.

sources.cite: Pierre Chaunu, Les Philippines et le Pacifique des Ibériques (1960)
Wikipedia: Sangley

flows.name: Hajj steamers from Bombay to Jeddah
flows.note: Steamers made the sea Hajj quick and crowded; British India regulated pilgrim ships after cholera outbreaks and the Kamaran quarantine station opened in 1882. Tens of thousands sailed from Bombay in a typical year. Ship counts are estimates.

sources.cite: John Slight, The British Empire and the Hajj, 1865-1956 (2015)
Wikipedia: Kamaran

flows.name: Abbasid dhows, Siraf to Guangzhou
flows.note: The Akhbar al-Sin wa'l-Hind (851) describes the run from Siraf to Guangzhou in about five legs over some months, timed to the monsoons; the Belitung wreck (c. 830) carried 60,000 Changsha bowls. Counts are estimates.

sources.cite: Akhbar al-Sin wa'l-Hind (851; Tim Mackintosh-Smith, trans., Two Arabic Travel Books, 2014)
Wikipedia: Belitung shipwreck
